6
A sprinter takes a time of 11.0 s to run a 100 m race. She first accelerates uniformly from rest,
reaching a speed of 10 m s–1. She then runs at a constant speed of 10 m s–1 until the finish line.
What is the uniform acceleration of the sprinter for the first part of the race?
A
0.5 m s–2
B
0.91 m s–2
C
1.7 m s–2
D
5.0 m s–2

hints: Notice the $100 \text{ m}$ is in two parts: an accelerating part from rest to $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and a constant-speed part at $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, with the two times adding to $11.0 \text{ s}$.
Connect the parts with distance: average speed while accelerating is $5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so if accelerating time is $t$ then $5t + 10(11.0 - t) = 100$.
First solve that distance equation for $t$ in $\text{s}$, then use $a = (v-u)/t$ with $v = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $u = 0$.
walkthrough: Let the uniform acceleration last a time $t$. Then the constant-speed running lasts $11.0 - t$ in $\text{s}$.
For uniform acceleration from rest to $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, average velocity is $(0+10)/2 = 5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so accelerating distance is $5t$ in $\text{m}$.
At constant $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, distance is $10(11.0 - t)$ in $\text{m}$. Total distance gives $5t + 10(11.0 - t) = 100$.
Use $a = (v - u)/t = (10 - 0)/2.0 = 5.0 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ with correct units. This is option D.

A.explanation: Too small because it treats the whole $100 \text{ m}$ as if covered at low average speed, not a short $2.0 \text{ s}$ acceleration to $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: This is $100/11.0 \approx 0.91$ with wrong units for acceleration; average speed for the whole race is not the acceleration of the first part.

C.explanation: Too small because it overestimates the accelerating time and distance, underestimating how quickly $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ must be reached to fit $100 \text{ m}$ in $11.0 \text{ s}$.

D.explanation: The accelerating time is $2.0 \text{ s}$, so $a = 10/2.0 = 5.0 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
